terms.gloss: an appointment, an arrangement to meet
evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.4: sī quod cōnstitūtum cum podagrā habēs (Lewis & Short s.v. cōnstituō)
terms.comment: The neuter of cōnstitūtus, “something agreed”. To have an appointment with someone is cōnstitūtum habēre cum aliquō.

terms.gloss: keep an appointment, come at the agreed time
evidence: Varr. RR 2.5.1; Cic. Caecin. 33 (Lewis & Short s.v. cōnstituō)

terms.gloss: make an appointment, arrange (a day, a meeting) with someone
terms.grammar: cum aliquō or with the dative of the person; with an accusative and infinitive or an indirect question for what is arranged
evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.2.65: cōnstituī cum hominibus quō diē mihi Messānae praestō essent
Cic. de Or. 1.265: vellem nōn cōnstituissem … mē hodiē ventūrum esse L. Aeliō
terms.comment: The verb of business Latin for fixing a day or a meeting with someone; the noun cōnstitūtum is its participle. Morgan–Owens gives hōram cōnstituere for making an appointment.

phrases.latin: sī quod cōnstitūtum cum podagrā habēs, fac ut in alium diem differās
phrases.english: if you have an appointment with your gout, put it off to another day
to have a date with someone

phrases.latin: cōnstituī cum hominibus quō diē mihi Messānae praestō essent
phrases.english: I arranged with the men a day on which they should meet me at Messana

phrases.latin: Cum medicō cōnstituī in crāstinum diem.
phrases.english: I’ve made an appointment with the doctor for tomorrow.
to make an appointment, fix a time
phrases.source: M-O s.v. appointment: make an appointment, make a date

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 93, 300.
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. appointment: make an appointment, make a date.
